title: Factors, Multiples, GCF & LCM
sub: Primes, factor pairs, greatest common factor, least common multiple

steps.html:
Factors & Multiples

Factors of 121, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12: divide into 12 evenly
Multiples of 1212, 24, 36, 48 …: the times table, forever
Factors are Few (they fit inside). Multiples are Many (they go on forever).
say: Today: factors and multiples.
Factors of twelve divide into twelve evenly: one, two, three, four, six, and twelve.
Multiples of twelve are its times table: twelve, twenty-four, thirty-six, and on forever.
Factors are few, they fit inside. Multiples are many, they go on forever.

steps.html:
Finding all factors: work in pairs

1 × 602 × 303 × 204 × 155 × 126 × 10

Stop when the pairs meet. 60 has 12 factors.

Primeexactly 2 factors: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 …
1 is not primeit has only 1 factor. 2 is the only even prime.
say: To find all the factors of sixty, list them in pairs: one and sixty, two and thirty, three and twenty, four and fifteen, five and twelve, six and ten.
Stop when the pairs meet in the middle. That's twelve factors.
A prime number has exactly two factors, one and itself. One is not prime. And two is the only even prime.

steps.html:
GCF = greatest common factor

42: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 21, 42
54: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, 27, 54
GCF(42, 54) = 6

Use it to split things into equal groups, or to simplify fractions.
say: The GCF is the biggest number that divides both.
List the factors of forty-two and fifty-four. The biggest one they share is six.
So the GCF is six.
Use the GCF when you split things into the largest equal groups, or when you simplify a fraction.

steps.html:
LCM = least common multiple

4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, 60
15: 15, 30, 45, 60
LCM(4, 15) = 60

Hot dogs in 4s, buns in 15s, same number of each? That's the LCM.
say: The LCM is the smallest number both go into.
Count by fifteens until you hit a multiple of four: fifteen, thirty, forty-five, sixty. Sixty works.
So the LCM of four and fifteen is sixty.
Use the LCM when two things repeat and you want them to line up, like hot dogs in packs of four and buns in packs of fifteen.

steps.html: Hot dogs come in packs of 6, buns in packs of 8. What is the smallest number of hot dogs you can buy to have the same number of buns?
say: Hot dogs come in packs of six, buns in packs of eight. What's the smallest number of hot dogs you can buy so you have the same number of buns?
steps.okSay: Yes! The least common multiple of six and eight is twenty-four.
steps.no: “Line up” = LCM. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. 24 is also a multiple of 6. Answer: 24.
steps.noSay: Not quite. This is a line-up question, so use the LCM. Count by eights: eight, sixteen, twenty-four. Twenty-four is also a multiple of six.

say: Great! Now 4 practice questions. You'll see the answer and an explanation after each one.
Last part: three checkpoint questions. Get two out of three to finish the lesson. You've got this!

steps.html:
Remember

1. Factors are few (fit inside). Multiples are many.

2. Find factors in pairs. 1 is not prime; 2 is the only even prime.

3. GCF: split into biggest equal groups. LCM: when things line up.
say: Let's review. Factors are few, multiples are many.
Find factors in pairs. One is not prime, and two is the only even prime.
Use the GCF to split into the biggest equal groups, and the LCM when things line up. Well done!
